bio.en: Gustaf Alstromer is a group partner at Y Combinator, where he has worked with 600+ startups, and previously started Airbnb's original growth team; he is also a driving force behind YC's focus on climate tech.
bio.zh: Gustaf Alstromer 是 Y Combinator 的集团合伙人，已辅导 600 多家初创公司，此前创办了 Airbnb 最初的增长团队；他也是 YC 聚焦气候科技的重要推动者。

summary.en: Gustaf boils startup failure down to one root cause—not talking to users, and therefore never finding product-market fit—and shares the most common mistakes YC founders make and the advice partners give most often. He covers the attributes of successful founders, why having a technical co-founder matters, and how YC's 'make things people want' still holds. The conversation also dives into climate tech: why momentum has shifted, what's new and exciting, and how to think about entering the space.
summary.zh: Gustaf 把创业失败归结为一个根本原因——不与用户交谈，因而永远找不到产品市场契合，并分享了 YC 创始人最常见的错误以及合伙人最常说起的建议。他谈到了成功创始人的共性、为何技术联合创始人至关重要，以及 YC 的“做人们想要的东西”为何至今成立。对话还深入气候科技：势头为何转变、有什么新鲜而令人兴奋的事，以及想进入这个领域该如何思考。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: If I drill down what makes companies fail, it's quite simple. It's just like they don't talk to users, which means they don't find product market fit. And if they don't find product market fit, nothing else really matters. What mistakes do people make is like it is all about that. It's all about talking to customers and learning that you're building something that's actually useful. YC Slack headline is make things people want, and it's still true and it's always going to be true.
turns.zh: 若要剖析导致公司失败的根本原因，其实很简单。核心问题在于他们不与用户沟通，因此无法找到产品与市场的契合点。而若无法实现产品与市场的契合，其他一切努力都将徒劳无功。人们常犯的错误往往归结于此——关键在于与客户沟通，了解用户真正需要的产品。YC Slack的口号是“打造人们真正想要的产品”，这句话至今仍不失其真理性，并且将永远是正确的准则。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. Honestly, it's so great to see you. I'm excited to be talking to you.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。说实话，能见到你真是太好了。能和你聊聊，我很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been looking forward to this conversation for a while ever since we booked this. We worked together at Airbnb for many years. I was really lucky to get to work with you before you moved on to bigger and better things at YC. Speaking of Airbnb, you once tweeted about how special an experience that was for you, and I think even more interestingly, how many of the people that have left Airbnb can't find another place that's as special that just like that bar has been set too high. And so my first question is just like, what do you think it was that made Airbnb so special? Why was it such an important experience for you and other people? And even more importantly, just what is it that you take from that experience that you bring to startups that you work with now?
turns.zh: 自从我们预定这次对话以来，我一直很期待这场交流。我们在Airbnb共事多年。在你转投YC开启更广阔事业之前，能与你共事，我深感荣幸。说到Airbnb，你曾在推特上提到那段经历对你意义非凡。更有趣的是，许多离开Airbnb的人都感叹，那里设定的标准太高，以至于很难找到同样特别的新工作。所以我的第一个问题是，你认为是什么让Airbnb如此特别？为什么它对你们以及其他人来说如此重要？更重要的是，你从那段经历中带走了哪些东西，并将其应用于现在合作的初创公司？

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Yeah, it's funny. I think this year in a couple of months it'll be 10 years ago since you and me started Airbnb.
turns.zh: 是啊，说来有趣。再过几个月，就是你和我创立Airbnb的十周年了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: It was 2012. The reason I treated that was I asked everyone that I'd met after Airbnb, because I had this experience of like, this was the highlight of my career up until then, at least being in the team like that and I asked everyone, "Have you found anything better?" Besides maybe one or two people, I haven't heard anybody say that they found something better. And they all missed that dearly. I thought a lot about why that was the case, but I would say Airbnb did not feel like a normal job. It felt like more like a group of friends trying to just do something together and we were friends. At least in the beginning it did not feel like this was a job. It was sort of like an ongoing project and an assembly of amazing people. I think in the end we managed to build two things, like a really successful company, thanks to Joe and Nate and Brian just for starting this. Without them there would be nothing to build. (00:06:04): I think people don't like to use the word family, but I feel like that way because when I go and meet with Airbnb alumnis from that team. We have a very special bond that reminds me of close social connections more than anything else. It does not remind me of coworkers. I asked myself why this was the case. The best answer I have is probably we brought in a special type of people. We had very diverse backgrounds. A lot of us was former founders. Not many of us were career people from the technology industry of the early days, not many of us. (00:06:37): I think that bar that we set, the first, I believe when I joined there was probably five or seven PMs and there was 30 engineers or something and you joined a little bit before me, those people set the bar or set the standard of what we were looking for afterwards. I think it took a long time to change that narrative. I mean, eventually you have to hire people that only had big corporation careers, but I don't remember we did that for a long time. When I actually read my goodbye note recently, my words there still means a lot to me and it means sort of like you're trying to reflect on exactly these things on like, building a great company that became successful and being part of this sort of family of really close friends.
turns.zh: 那是2012年。我之所以特别关注这段经历，是因为我在Airbnb之后遇到的每个人，都曾问过他们：“你找到比Airbnb更好的工作了吗？”除了个别例外，其他人都说找不到。他们都无比怀念那段时光。我曾深思其中的原因，但我认为Airbnb不像普通工作。它更像是一群朋友试图共同完成某件事，我们就是朋友。至少在最初，它不像是一份工作。它更像是一个持续的项目，汇聚了众多杰出人才。我认为最终我们成功打造了两样东西——一家非常成功的公司，这要归功于乔、内特和布莱恩的创业初心。没有他们，就没有什么可以搭建的。（00:06:04）：我知道人们不喜欢用‘家庭’这个词，但我就是这么觉得的。当我去见Airbnb那个团队的校友时，我们之间有一种特殊的纽带，比起同事关系更像亲密的朋友。我问自己为什么会这样。我能想到的最好的答案是，我们吸引了特别类型的人才。我们背景各异。团队里很多人曾是创业者，但早期科技行业的职业人士却很少。（00:06:37）：我认为我们设定的那个标准，第一个标准是，我加入时大概有五到七位产品经理，30位工程师左右，而你比我稍早加入的人，他们为后来者树立了标杆。我认为改变这种叙事花了很长时间。最终你不得不招聘那些只有大公司工作经验的人，但我不记得我们这么做过很久。当我最近读到自己的告别信时，我写的那些话对我意义非凡，它们让我反思正是在这些方面——打造一家成功的伟大公司，成为这个由亲密朋友组成的大家庭的一员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it sounds like if you had to boil down what Airbnb did, it sounds like hiring was the main piece that impacted the way it turned out just like the founders being very specific about the type of people they were hiring.
turns.zh: 听起来如果要概括Airbnb的成功秘诀，招聘策略无疑是关键因素之一——创始人对招聘人才的严格把关至关重要。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that's like, I don't know, a take away there of just what you recommend to founders, like hiring. People know, be very careful who you hire. The first, I don't know, 10 people will impact the culture long term. But I don't know. Is there anything just abstracting away there of just what to look for in that first batch of hires?
turns.zh: 有没有什么经验值得总结，比如说对创始人有什么建议，比如招聘问题。大家都知道，聘用合适的人至关重要。前10名员工会对公司文化产生长期影响，但具体该怎么做呢？

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: It's a tricky one because I would like to say that all the things that we did were the cost of the outcome of this, but that's not really how the world works. Some of the things we did work, some of the things that we did did not work. It's hard for us to actually disentangle what those things are, but I think we can talk about the things that we did. First of all, we made sure we hired people that were really excited to be there, right? They wanted to build Airbnb and they were really excited to work on Airbnb. That was the most important thing. Of course people had other offers, but I think you can figure out from those offers are you excited to be here or not. So that was probably the first thing. (00:08:30): The second thing I think is trying to understand the true motivations of the people that were there, like lower, "Why are you here?" We did something we call culture interviews that I think the founders have written about or there's probably content online about this. We did a lot of culture interviews early on to try to figure out we got the people that were there that mapped our core values and were really excited to work on Airbnb. I think finally, I don't know how this happened, we did pick people from diverse backgrounds. Most startups don't have most of the PMs being former founders, but I believe that was the case for the first 10 or 12 or 15 PMs at Airbnb. A lot of us were former founders. I think that that made a big difference for how you make decisions and how you get started on things. (00:09:21): I think I actually see this a lot in the Airbnb founders. They really care about the time at YC and they tried to recreate YC inside Airbnb a couple of times with demo day and with so new products completely isolated from the rest, starting with doing things that don't scale and talking to customers. So I think that that experience had made a big impact on them, but it's hard to say just these two things go and apply these things. It's actually kind of hard to say, "Well that will work at it as Airbnb." I think that's a really tricky question to answer. (00:09:51): The last thing I would say is Airbnb had an incredible business model, an incredible business from early on and it was hard to fail. What I mean by that is it's hard to fail with a company. You can fail with individual things inside the company, but a company was still going to succeed. I think we all felt that. A lot of companies don't have the ability to take risks like Airbnb did early on because they don't have something that's so obviously great.
turns.zh: 这确实是个棘手的问题。我本想说我们所做的所有决策都是为了最终的成功铺路，但现实并非如此。有些措施奏效了，有些则适得其反。我们很难理清其中的因果关系，但至少可以谈谈我们采取的措施。首先，我们确保招聘的人员对加入Airbnb充满热情。他们渴望参与Airbnb的建设，并为此激情满满。这是最重要的考量。当然，候选人可能还有其他 offer，但通过这些 offer，你能判断他们是否真心想来 Airbnb。（00:08:30）第二点是深入挖掘员工的真实动机。比如问他们：“你为什么来这里？”我们开展了所谓的“文化访谈”（culture interviews），创始人曾对此进行过阐述，网上也应该有相关内容。早期我们通过多次文化访谈，确保入职员工既认同我们的核心价值观，又对在 Airbnb 工作充满热情。我觉得最后，虽然不确定具体如何做到的，但我们确实成功招募了背景多元的人才。大多数初创公司的高级产品经理都曾是创始人，但 Airbnb 的前10到12位产品经理几乎都是如此。我们中的许多人都是前创始人。我认为这对决策和项目启动方式产生了深远影响。（00:09:21）我觉得Airbnb的创始人身上有很多值得借鉴的特质。他们非常重视在YC的经历，并试图在Airbnb内部复刻YC的模式，比如举办Demo Day，以及让新产品在初期与其他部门隔离，专注于做不易规模化的事情、倾听用户反馈等。我认为这种经历对他们影响深远，但要将这些经验直接应用到Airbnb的具体案例中并非易事。（00:09:51）最后我想说，Airbnb从一开始就拥有令人惊叹的商业模式，成功的可能性极高。我指的是这家公司很难失败。公司内部的某些项目可能会失败，但整体方向不会偏离。我们都深有体会。很多公司没有Airbnb早期那样的冒险精神，因为他们没有那么明显的成功蓝图。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really interesting point on the last piece that you may have the most amazing culture and hire incredibly well, but if the company doesn't work out, it's not going to be looked back as like, "Wow, that was an amazing experience, but we failed."
turns.zh: 关于你刚刚提到的最后一个观点——即便你拥有最棒的文化、招聘了最出色的团队，但如果公司最终失败了，人们也不会回首说"哇，那真是一段超棒的经历，可惜我们最终失败了"——这确实很有意思。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's interesting. So you mentioned YC and this kind of is a good segue to where I want to focus most of our time. You mentioned that you've worked with over 600 companies at this point, which is absurd. It feels like it's you get some statistical significance on takeaways at this point of what works and doesn't work. So I have just a bunch of questions about your experience working at YC and with all these companies. The first is I think about this quote that Elad Gill tweeted once and he wrote, I think, a post about it. Elad Gill is a legendary angel investor. He said that starting a company is an act of desperation. You're either desperate to change the trajectory of your career or you're desperate to make a bunch of money, you're desperate to achieve some kind of mission or build a specific product that you're just like, "I need this to exist." I'm curious if you agree with that sentiment and then I have a follow-up question around that.
turns.zh: 嗯，确实很有意思。你提到过YC，这里正好可以顺便聊聊我最想深入探讨的主题。你说目前已经与600多家公司合作过，这数字太惊人了。感觉你已经能从中总结出一些关于成功与失败的规律。所以我对在YC工作以及与这么多公司合作的经历有很多疑问。首先，我想起Elad Gill曾在推特上提到的观点，他还写过一篇相关的博文。Elad Gill是传奇天使投资人，他说创办公司往往源于绝望——要么是迫切想改变职业轨迹，要么是急于赚大钱，或是想实现某种使命或打造特定产品。不知你是否认同这种观点？然后我还有后续的问题想问。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Yeah, actually I haven't heard it before, but you know me, I'm an optimistic person. I think it probably reflects on my view of this question, but I would say desperation sounds like a negative place that you're starting at. I actually think that most people to start companies start from a positive place. But the motivations, I agree with what he said, can be very diverse for successful founders, right? (00:11:41): So we actually asked this in one of the early Group Office Hours sessions. We asked them, "Why are you doing this?" And we don't want to hear an answer like, "I found this niche of the market.' That's not the why. The why is like, "Why will you come in and work late after four years when you have no money left and everything's going to shit?", right? Then the niche market is not the answer. There's something deeper than that. We've learned that it varies a lot for people's motivations to start companies. Some of them just want to solve some technical problem that they feel are passionate about solving. Some of them want to prove themselves in front of others or prove themselves towards themselves. Some have grand really important motivations to change the world and they will say things like, "I want to give everyone water or I want to solve climate change or I want to democratize publishing." You can imagine any number of large ideas. Some people just want to start a big company and just want to be successful. (00:12:44): It doesn't matter, in my experience, what your motivation is. I don't think either of these motivations. It sounds like some of them will be better than others. In my experience, it's not the case. The motivation will change over time to just running this thing, right? Like once something becomes big, it's hard to think every day about exactly why you got started because the motivation is just like it can be fun and work on boring things because it's fun to build something big. Everything doesn't have to be shiny and big and grandiose because there are many ideas that are "boring," but just the idea of running the company becomes the motivation eventually.
turns.zh: 嗯，实际上我之前没听过这个观点，但你知道我是个乐观主义者。我觉得这可能反映了我对这个问题的看法。不过说真的，绝望听起来像是创办公司时的负面出发点。我认为大多数创业者都是从积极的初衷出发的。但我同意他说的，成功的创始人动机确实各不相同，对吧？（00:11:41）我们在早期Group Office Hours的会议上就问过这个问题："你们为什么要做这件事？"我们不想听到"我发现了某个细分市场"的回答。这不是核心原因。真正的问题应该是："四年后没钱了，一切都要崩盘时，你为什么还会继续加班？"细分市场不是答案。背后有更深层的动机。我们发现人们创业的动机千差万别。有些人只想解决自己热衷的技术难题；有些人想向他人或自己证明自己；有些人怀揣着改变世界的宏伟愿景，比如"我想让每个人都能用上水""我想解决气候变化问题""我想让出版民主化"等等。这类宏大构想不胜枚举。还有些人只想创办大公司，追求成功。（00:12:44）但以我的经验来看，动机并不重要。我不认为某种动机比其他更好。在我看来，动机会随时间演变，最终归结为运营公司本身。例如，当公司规模做大后，人们很难每天反思最初的创业初衷，因为动机已经演变为享受运营乐趣、专注于枯燥工作，因为构建大公司的过程本身就充满乐趣。并非所有创意都必须光鲜亮丽、宏伟壮观，许多看似"枯燥"的想法同样值得运营，最终动机也会回归到公司运营本身。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting that one of the main things you look for, it sounds like when you're interviewing, is how strong and durable is that drive to build this company. Is that what you're saying?
turns.zh: 真有意思，你提到在面试中最看重的一点，是创始人建立公司的动力有多强、多持久。您是这个意思吗？

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: It's actually kind of hard for screen for motivation, I would say, in interviews because the purpose of this kind of Office Hour question is to highlight why someone is there and highlight the diversity of reasons people are there and sometimes even highlight from one founder to another co-founder why they are doing this. They might have never talked about this. Actually, surprisingly, often founders have not talked about why they're doing this. And just knowing why someone is here really helps with conflict resolution for example, really helps with understanding why someone is there on a certain day or something like that. So it's not something we screen for as much as I think we try to help founders discover this among themself and really know this about themself. I've just accepted that the motivations to start companies is widely diverse.
turns.zh: 其实在面试中筛选动机挺难的，因为Office Hour环节的目的是突出创始人为何选择创业，展现他们的多样性，有时甚至要让创始人互相讲述创业初衷。这些话题他们可能从未提及。令人惊讶的是，创始人往往对自己的创业动机语焉不详。比如，了解创始人的初衷对化解冲突很有帮助，能理解他们为何在某天选择创业之类的。所以我们不怎么筛选动机，更倾向于帮助创始人自己挖掘内在动机。我已经接受了创业动机千差万别的现实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you ever discourage founders from starting a company when you see that maybe it won't be a durable kind of lasting motivation or whatever other reasons just knowing how hard starting a company ends up being?
turns.zh: 当您发现创始人可能缺乏持久的动机，或者存在其他问题时，会劝阻他们创业吗？比如，创业可能并非自然的职业晋升之路。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: It's a good question. I would say sometimes if someone doesn't have a motivation or don't know why they're doing this, they're doing this because they read that it would be a natural career step. So a good reason to not start a company is if you think of starting a company as a career step. Well, it is not. Because if it's successful, it'll be your entire career. It'll be 10 years most likely. And if it's not successful, then it's not something that people generally aspire to start. So non-successful startups. So I think people will start companies because this is sort of something they want to put on their resume. They have not understood what startups are or why you should do them. (00:14:58): Sometimes you can screen and kind of figure this out, but sometimes people don't even know why they're starting a company when they get started and it kind of gets figured out along the way. And that's okay. I don't want to discourage people who don't know exactly why they're starting this company just to start a company. They might figure out along the way and find the true motivation after doing this for a little bit or finding that it's really fun. (00:15:21): I think I discourage people to start startups if they have so many other things that are important than their life that are more important than the startup. So if there are financial constraints or family constraints or relationship constraints and they are going to trump this, then yeah, you should think a second time perhaps because startups are hard. They're much harder than a normal job. Equally hard if they're successful or failure, right? There's no middle way, we're like, "Oh, my company is doing great so I can chill." That doesn't work that way either. So I don't really discourage or encourage people, I just want them to have all the information.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。我觉得有时候创始人没有明确动机，或者不清楚自己为何创业，可能只是因为听说创业是职业晋升的必经之路。但这种想法是错误的。如果创业成功，它将成为你全部事业，可能持续十年；如果失败，那就不是人们理想中的创业之路了。所以很多创业失败的案例。人们创业可能只是为了在简历上添彩，却不了解创业的真谛或动机。（00:14:58）有时通过筛选能发现问题，但有时创始人创业时甚至不清楚动机，而是在过程中逐渐领悟。这没关系。我不会劝阻那些不清楚动机的人创业，他们或许会在过程中找到真正的动力。（00:15:21）我会劝阻那些生活中有比创业更重要的事务（财务压力、家庭羁绊、感情纠葛）的人创业。如果这些问题压倒性存在，就该三思了。创业太难了，比普通工作难得多，无论成功还是失败都一样艰辛，没有中间路径。以为“公司发展顺利就能轻松”的想法也是错的。所以我不劝阻也不鼓励，只想让他们掌握所有信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned YC Office Hours and I had a question around this. I'm working on this piece where I'm interviewing a bunch of B2B founders of companies that are doing super well and I asked them a few questions like, "How'd you come up with the idea? How'd you find your first few customers?" it's shocking how many of them bring up a conversation in YC Office Hours as the most pivotal point that set them on the trajectory that they're on now. I'm curious what happens in these Office Hours? What are the most common pieces of advice that you give or maybe most surprising pieces of advice that you give in these Office Hours so that people can get maybe a glimpse into these conversations you have?
turns.zh: 你提到了YC的办公时间，我对此有个疑问。我正在撰写一篇报道，采访了许多发展势头极佳的B2B初创公司创始人，并向他们提了几个问题，比如“你是如何想出这个创意的？你是如何找到首批客户的？”令人惊讶的是，其中许多人都将YC办公时间视为他们事业发展轨迹的关键转折点。我很好奇这些办公时间里都发生了什么？你们在那里给出的最常见建议是什么？或者说，有哪些最令人惊讶的建议？这样读者或许能一窥你们在这些对话中所探讨的内容。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: So at YC we have two type of Office Hours, two of the common ones. We have regular Office Hours, which is usually a one-on-one or basically the founders talking to me, or me plus another partner. They happen every week or every other week throughout the entire program. And they happen years after the program on the regular basis. Then we have Group Office Hours, which is you and six or seven other startups talking to us. They have [inaudible 00:17:07] a little bit different purpose. So the goal of the regular Office Hour, I always ask the question, "What's holding you back from moving faster? We don't want to hear updates, we don't want to hear strategy questions. We want to understand what's slowing you down or what's holding you back from moving even faster. You generally have a specific goal." (00:17:27): And I think that question of what's slowing you down or were holding you back crystallizes the priorities. There are only so many things you can do as a startup and there are only so many things that matters at that stage. And by asking that question, we can start digging into, "Okay, what's the goal? What are the things that drives towards that goal? What are the things that's slowing you down towards that goal?" Usually, the founders don't know what's slowing it down, so the conversation and us probing questions actually leads to us or them discovering what it is just slowing them down. (00:17:59): In the Group Office Hour, it's a little bit different. The Group Office Hour holds a couple of different purposes. One of them is if I think back on Paul and Jessica's motivation to start YC, this is a surprise to them, but starting a company is incredibly lonely. You can't really lean on your employees and say, "Hey, I'm feeling really shitty as a founder today. Everything is going to shit." Employees isn't going to take that well. So you lean on perhaps your investors, but they're not really available. But what you can lean on is other founders because they're all in the same situation. It's sort of like when you ask a founder the question, "How are things going?", it's so emotional for them to answer that question because it's never going well, right? It's never like, "Oh, everything is going fantastic." They might say that, but everybody knows all founders, when they look each other's eyes, then no, that's not the answer. (00:18:48): So founders have infinite number of problems that they're thinking about all the time, which is why they're allergic to the question, "How are things going?" But when YC started, we put all the founders in a group together in a room and they started learning that all founders, all companies are broken in some way, right? They're all having these massive problems and they're all feeling that anxiety when they hear the question, "How are things going?" And just hearing other founders explain their problems, perhaps solving their problems, is a really good way for yourself to both feel motivated to do it yourself and see how problems get solved when other companies are having similar problems. Nowadays because of the scale at YC, we group companies together that have the same problems or the same area that they're operating in. (00:19:30): The second thing that Group Office Hours do well is accountability, right? We ask you, "What were your goals? What were your goals for the last two weeks? Did you hit them?" And then that gives founders accountability because founders are competitive. They don't want to look bad. They don't want to come back after two weeks and say "Nothing worked," or at least like, "We didn't learn anything." They want to learn something and make progress whether it's positive or negative. (00:19:54): Group Office Hours to me is the most magical moment because it really creates this very intense three or four month period. Founders often come back to us afterwards and say, "Hey, we want to do that again. We don't have this really intense, really productive period. We don't have a program exactly. We have other programs, but we don't have anything exactly that mimics that experience." But we do encourage founders to continue with Group Office Hours after YC. Many of them do and many of them, ad hoc, continue to meet for years in this group setting where they ask the same kind of questions to each other, to hold themselves accountable, to learn from each other, and to just have someone else to lean on. I think this was unknown and somehow the world didn't know before that starting company is super lonely and you have all these anxiety. By just talking to other people who have the same problems, it's just one of the best thing you can do.
turns.zh:
因此，在YC，我们有两种类型的办公时间，其中最常见的两种是常规办公时间和小组办公时间。常规办公时间通常是一对一的交流，或者是创始人与我，或者是创始人与另一位合伙人之间的对话。这种会议每周或每两周举行一次，贯穿整个项目期间，甚至在项目结束多年后也会定期举行。而小组办公时间则不同，你和其他六七家初创公司一起参与讨论，目的有所不同。  

常规办公时间的核心问题是：“是什么在阻碍你加速前进？”我们不想听汇报，也不想听战略问题，我们想了解是什么在拖慢你的脚步，或者阻碍你更快地发展。通常创始人都有一个明确的目标。（00:17:27）我认为“是什么在阻碍你前进？”这个问题能清晰地聚焦优先事项。初创公司能做的事情有限，处于这个阶段重要的事情也有限。通过这个问题，能帮助我们深入探讨：“你的目标是什么？推动目标实现的关键因素是什么？阻碍你达成目标的因素是什么？” 通常创始人并不知道是什么在拖慢进程，所以对话和我们的追问能帮助他们发现阻碍因素。  

小组办公时间则有所不同。它有几个不同的目的。其中之一是回想保罗和杰西卡创立YC的初衷时会发现，这对他们来说是个惊喜——创办公司其实非常孤独。你无法向员工倾诉：“作为创始人，今天我感觉糟透了。一切都乱套了。” 员工不会善意接受这种抱怨。但你可以向其他创始人求助，因为他们都处于相同的境地。比如当你问创始人“情况如何？”时，他们会情绪激动地回答，因为情况从不顺利，对吧？他们可能会说一切顺利，但所有创始人都知道，当他们互相对视时，大家都知道这不是真相。  

（00:18:48）创始人总有无数的难题需要时刻思考，这也是他们对“情况如何？”这个问题避之不及的原因。但YC创立之初，我们把所有创始人聚集在一起，他们开始意识到所有创始人、所有公司都存在或多或少的缺陷。大家都面临着重大挑战，听到“情况如何？”这个问题时都会感到焦虑。亲眼目睹其他创始人解决问题，也能激励自己去行动，同时了解类似问题的解决之道。如今，由于YC的规模扩大，会将面临相同问题或处于相同业务领域的公司分组讨论。  

小组办公时间的另一个重要作用是责任追究。我们会问：“你们的目标是什么？过去两周的目标达成了吗？” 这能让创始人承担责任，因为他们天生好胜，不愿出丑。不想两周后回来说“毫无进展”，或者至少不想让别人知道自己无能为力。
“我们什么都没学到。”他们希望通过学习获得进步，无论是积极的还是消极的收获。（00:19:54）：对我来说，“团体办公时间”是最神奇的时刻，因为它真正造就了那段长达三四个月的高强度学习期。很多创始人事后会回来对我们说：“嘿，我们想再经历一次那种状态。我们现在没有这样高强度、高产出的阶段了。虽然我们也有其他项目，但没有一个能完全复刻那种体验。”不过我们确实鼓励创始人在完成YC项目后继续开展“团体办公时间”。许多人确实这么做了，还有不少人会临时组织小组会议，持续多年。他们会在这种集体环境中互相提问、互相监督、相互学习，彼此借力。这让我意识到，创办公司其实是一件非常孤独的事，充满各种焦虑感。而与那些正面临相同挑战的人交流，恰恰是能获得巨大助力的最佳方式之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many things that come up when you talk about this. One is I had a startup at one point and we worked in the coworking space. We joined the coworking space because we're like, "Oh, we'll meet other founders. It'll be social, we won't be alone." But it turns out everyone's just heads down, headphones on, "I don't have time for anything. I just need to work." It's like a microcosm of that experience that even if you're surrounded by founders, no one has time to do anything. They're just working.
turns.zh: 谈到这个话题，脑海中涌现出诸多回忆。其中之一是我曾创办一家初创公司，当时我们入驻了共享办公空间。选择那里是因为我们心想：“能结识其他创业者，一起社交，避免孤单。”但结果发现，每个人都埋头工作，戴着耳机，“忙得不可开交，根本无暇他顾”。这仿佛是那种孤独感的缩影——即便身处创业者群体中，大家也无暇交流，始终专注于工作。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: You got to schedule it and force it and put the laptops on the floor and the phones on the floor and you just sit there with pen and paper. That's how you have to do it. We tried to mimic that as much as we could over Zoom. But honestly the best experience of this was in person, in a ring, in mountain view with no computers and everyone just paying attention to everyone. That was the best experience. Yeah, that's what I remember is one of the most meaningful parts of YC. I didn't have it myself when I did YC, but now everyone has it.
turns.zh: 你必须主动安排时间，强制执行，收起笔记本电脑和手机，拿起纸笔静心专注。这才是有效的做法。我们曾试图在Zoom会议上模拟这种氛围，但最棒的体验还是面对面交流——在山景城的圆桌会议上，大家放下手机，专心聆听。这才是最难忘的YC经历。我参加YC时没有这样的体验，但如今所有人都经历过了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing that's made me think about is someone tweeted once, "Don't ever ask a founder how they're doing or how it's going. It just creates all this anxiety because nothing's ever going great."
turns.zh: 还有一件事让我深有感触，有人曾发推文：“千万别问创业者进展如何或情况怎样。这只会引发焦虑，因为从来没有什么事进展顺利的。”

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Don't do it. Everybody looks at each other's eyes and they know that they're allergic to that question.
turns.zh: 别这么做。大家四目相对，都明白这个问题会引发不适。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's hilarious. So just to summarize the questions you said you asked, the one is in the individual Office Hours, is what's holding you back. And then in the group setting, what was the question again that you asked?
turns.zh: 太逗了。总结一下你提到的两个问题：一是在单独办公时间里，问他们阻碍进展的因素；二是在集体会议上，问他们过去两周的目标完成情况，以及未达成目标的原因。简单明了。通过分享阻碍因素和达成目标的秘诀，能让同处一室的其他七家初创公司受益匪浅。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: What are your goals for next two weeks and what were your goals for the last two weeks and did you hit the goals? And if you didn't hit them, what came in the way of hitting the goals? It's very simple. That can uncover lots of problems that other founders are having exactly in the same way. Just by talking about the things that held you back or the things that allowed you to hit your goals, uncover something material for the other seven companies doing that in the ring.
turns.zh: 如果退后一步，审视你接触过的初创公司，你认为早期阶段创业者最常犯的错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you kind of zoomed out a little bit and thought about the startups you've worked with, what would you say are the most common mistakes that early stage startups make broadly?
turns.zh: 太多了。说真的，我最初了解创业就是通过谷歌搜索，偶然发现保罗·格雷厄姆的文章，因为他总是在写这些内容——

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: There's so many. I mean, this is how I initially learned about startups, by searching for that on Google and landing on Paul Graham's articles because he kept-
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: I think I've written many articles about this topic because it is so common. So this topic can go on forever. But if I take the most recent experience I've had in YC, I would say startups fail, one, because they don't talk to customers. And if you don't talk to customers or users, you don't actually know what's important. If you don't know what's important, it doesn't matter what you build, it doesn't matter kind of what ideas you have in your head if you don't actually know what it is that you need to build and you don't validate with customers. That's where a lot of the failure stems from. A lot of early YC for us or early part of the program is us pushing and probing founders to be like, "Tell us about the conversations you've had with the customers. What did you learn? Can you show us the organizations?" Or like all these questions, like, "What are the software they're using? What are they paying for? What problems do they have? How are they describing the intensity of that problem?" So that's what we spent a lot of time early at YC. (00:23:43): After that, I would say one of the commons mistakes in... I'm not talking about generally startups here, I'm talking inside YC. The second most common thing I see in YC is people are just afraid to talk to customers. They're just not trying hard enough to get in front of customers. I think this comes from, technical people tend to think that software is just sort of solution to everything. But really what you should need to do is to talk to someone over Zoom or over phone or in person, even better. People are just afraid of doing that and they're afraid of being rejected. These are common, people that want to build good products are just really afraid of people saying no. (00:24:25): The problem is, which anyone who hasn't done sales before that joined YC, they realize this, is that if you take the average customer group in the world, 90% are not early adopters. It doesn't matter if you have something new and cool, they're just not interested. They are not incentivized to take risks in their job to try something new. They're just incentivized to not take risks and just continue what they're doing. Those 10 percents are the early adopters. They're The ones that you actually want to reach. But that means you have to reach 10 to find one. And then you convince that one person to get on the phone or a video call with you. And that takes work and it takes a lot of work. I think people don't really think of this. This is common knowledge, basic stuff for salespeople, but founders should never done sales before just get surprised by the percentages and the sort of what it means to do this. (00:25:12): If I think of more generally outside of YC, so these are two kind of things I experience within YC, but I think generally outside of YC, I would say the two most common problems the same one is not talking to customers, the other one is not being technical and not knowing what it takes to build successful technology company. It means having technical founders and it means being able to build the first prototype. This is something we screen for when we interview people in YC and we aren't accepting a whole lot of team that don't know how to build or get their first prototype built themselves because we know it is a super common value pattern. (00:25:50): I can go on and on and on and on for this one, but honestly if I drill down what makes companies fail, it's quite simple. It's just like they don't talk to users, which means they don't find product market fit. And if they don't find product market fit, nothing else really matters. What mistakes do people make is it is all about that. It's all about talking to customers and learning that you're building something that's actually useful. YC Slack headline is make things people want, and it's still true and it's always going to be true.
turns.zh:
我觉得我写过很多关于这个话题的文章，因为它实在太常见了。所以这个话题可以永远聊下去。但如果我以最近在YC的经历为例，我会说创业公司失败的原因之一，是因为他们不去和客户交流。如果你不和客户或用户对话，你就根本不了解什么才是重要的。如果你连什么重要都不知道，那无论你建什么产品，无论你脑子里有什么想法，如果你不去验证客户需求，那都是徒劳的。这正是很多失败的根源所在。在YC早期阶段，我们会反复敦促创始人去和客户交流："告诉我们和客户的对话内容，你们学到了什么？能让我们看看他们的组织架构吗？"诸如此类的问题，比如"他们用的是什么软件？他们为哪些服务付费？他们面临哪些问题？他们如何描述问题的紧迫性？"这些都是我们在YC早期阶段花费大量时间关注的点。（00:23:43）：接下来，我要说另一个常见错误——我这里说的不是一般创业公司，而是YC里的情况。YC里最常见的错误之一，就是人们不敢去和客户交流。他们没有足够的勇气去接触客户。我认为这源于技术人员倾向于认为软件是解决一切问题的万能钥匙。但实际上，你需要做的是通过Zoom、电话或者面对面交流去和用户对话。人们害怕被拒绝，害怕被否定。这些都是常见的心理障碍——那些想打造优质产品的人，就是害怕听到客户说“不”。（00:24:25）：问题在于，任何没做过销售却加入YC的人都会意识到，全球90%的客户群体都不是早期采用者。你即便有再酷炫的新产品，他们也无动于衷。他们没有动力去冒险尝试新事物，只想按部就班。只有10%的客户是早期采用者，他们才是你真正需要触达的对象。但这意味着你要接触10个客户才能找到一个。而要说服这个客户和你通电话或视频通话，又需要付出大量努力。我觉得人们对此缺乏认识。这对销售人员来说是常识，但没做过销售的创始人往往会被这些比例和背后的逻辑惊到。（00:25:12）：如果把话题扩展到YC之外，我在YC里遇到的两个问题同样适用于外部环境：一是缺乏客户沟通，二是缺乏技术能力，不懂如何打造成功的科技公司。这意味着创始人必须具备技术背景，还要能完成第一个原型。这也是我们在YC面试时筛选的关键指标，我们不接受很多不懂得如何开发原型、自己都做不出来的团队，因为我们深知这是一种极其常见的失败模式。（00:25:50）：关于这个话题我可以讲个没完，但说实话，如果深挖创业公司失败的原因，其实很简单。就是他们不去和用户交流，导致无法找到产品市场匹配点。如果找不到产品市场匹配点，无论你建什么产品，无论你脑子里有什么想法，都徒劳无功。
产品是否好用，这才是最重要的。人们常犯的错误往往出于此。关键在于与客户交流，了解他们真正需要什么，从而打造出真正有用的产品。YC Slack的口号是“做出人们想要的东西”，这句话至今仍适用，未来也将永远正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really interesting and good advice. It's interesting that... Like, "Talk to customers," people hear that all the time. They're like, "Of course we're going to talk to customers. We're going to do that of course." And your experience is they know this but they just don't do it probably because they're afraid. Maybe also because they think they already know what they need to build and it's like, "Yeah, we're good."
turns.zh: 这真是很有趣的建议。很有意思的是……比如，“去和客户聊聊”，人们老是听到这句话。他们会说：“我们当然会和客户沟通啊。这是理所当然的啊。”但你的经验表明，他们明明知道这一点却不去做，可能是因为害怕。或许还因为他们觉得自己已经清楚需要开发的产品，所以就自以为是地说：“我们已经做得很棒了。”

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: And you have all these validators, right? So the people are validating that even if you don't talk to customers, why has he accepted you? This investor invested in you. This investor said you were great, like blah blah blah. All these different validations that you confuse with product market fit, right? We have to remind everyone on the first day in YC, "None of you have product market fit because you probably don't," right? Almost nobody has. Because people confuse this external validation with the thing that matters the most, which is talking to customers and learning what matters. It's just like a thing that just keeps coming back. Some get really good at it. And that is the source of successful startups, is when you really get good at this.
turns.zh: 还有那些验证者，对吧？所以人们会质疑，即便你不去和客户交流，那个投资者为什么会投资你呢？那个投资者说你很棒，等等等等。这些外部验证的标准，你会把它们和产品市场契合度混为一谈，对吧？我们在YC第一天就得提醒所有人：“你们谁都没有产品市场契合度，因为你们很可能没有。”几乎没人有。因为人们把这种外部验证和最重要的环节——去和客户交流、了解用户需求——搞混了。这就是个循环往复的问题。有些人很擅长这一点。而成功的创业公司往往就是在这一点上做得好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me coming back to Airbnb, one of the most important moments in Airbnb history was Paul Graham telling the founders of Airbnb, "Where are your customers?" And they're like, "Oh, they're in New York" and he's like, "Why are you talking to me and not in New York right now talking to them?" And they talk about that all the time.
turns.zh: 这让我想起Airbnb的例子。Airbnb历史上最重要的时刻之一，是保罗·格雷厄姆对创始人说的“你们的客户在哪里？”他们回答“哦，他们在纽约啊”，然后他反问“那你为什么不去纽约和他们交流，而来和我聊天？”他们现在还经常提起这件事。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Yeah, it's absolutely true. I think he wrote the article Do Things That Don't Scale as a learning.... The learning there was the Airbnb founders doing the trips to New York and learning about how to build Airbnb, which is a very counterintuitive idea, which is when you have to spend the most amount of time with your customers. I think Airbnb is sort of one of the best stories inside YC of doing this well.
turns.zh: 是啊，这完全正确。我记得他写《做那些不可扩展的事》这篇文章，目的是让创业者明白……其中的核心启示是Airbnb的创始人亲自去纽约，了解如何打造Airbnb。这是个非常反直觉的做法，因为你必须花最多时间和客户在一起。我认为Airbnb是YC里在这方面做得最成功的案例之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This also reminds me, I've been talking to a bunch of founders recently. I asked them, "How many customers have you talked to help figure out this idea?" So just the other day it was 150 financial CROs that they talked to before they actually started raising this round. Another company, actually two Airbnb guys that started, they actually ran ads I think on LinkedIn to find specific people to talk to and that specific role. And they talked to probably at least 100, maybe 200. So there's a strong correlation there.
turns.zh: 这也让我想起最近和很多创始人交流的经历。我问他们：“为了验证这个想法，你们和多少客户交流过？”前几天，有个公司在融资前找了150位金融CRO做访谈。还有个公司，两个Airbnb出身的创始人，他们在LinkedIn上投放广告，专门找特定职位的人交流。可能他们至少找了100到200个人。可见这两者之间有很强的关联。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's the volumes that people don't expect. They think they might have to talk to five, but I think you have to talk to 25 to 50. That means you have to reach out to a lot more to be able to get to people that are potentially early adopters. Those ones you talk to are also the ones that become your customers. So you are already doing most of the sales by just doing this work anyway.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得大家低估了交流的数量。他们以为只需要和五个人聊聊，但实际上你得和25到50个人沟通。这样才能接触到那些潜在的早期用户。而你交流过的这些人，往往也会成为你的客户。所以只要你肯下功夫，就能完成大部分销售工作了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have maybe one tactical tip you could share of just either getting over your fear of talking to customers or just holding yourself accountable to actually doing it?
turns.zh: 你有没有什么实用的技巧，可以帮助人们克服和客户交流的恐惧，或者督促自己去行动？

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Yeah, I tell this story, I actually told this story yesterday. So remember when you sign up first service that's a cool service and you hear about in TechCrunch or something like that and then you realize you already signed up a year ago, right? And then from the founder's perspective, you sign up to something you never used it. So the founders who build those services, their inclination to think is that "Everybody hates me because they sign up and they never use me." They never use the service. The fear of that is that basically the fear of rejection. So if I put my thing out there and most people won't use it and they will tell all their friends how shitty this thing is, you should never even sign up for it, that's the fear people have, but the truth is that people sign up for it and be like, "Oh, I'm busy. I got something else to do." And they actually don't remember or care. (00:29:43): So whenever you sign for something that you signed up a year ago, think of yourself that that is the common customer experience, which is that you just sign up for a lot of stuff you don't even remember you. You never have this, "I hate this thing' reaction. You always have this like, "I'm indifferent to this thing. I don't actually care to even complete the sign up flow or try it out," right? I think that's the thing that people need to remember, is that the worst thing that can happen to startup is not that people hate what you're doing, it's that they're completely indifferent to what you're doing. It's not the worst thing, but the most common thing that happens is people just is indifferent. But it doesn't give you a second chance. Let's say, it always gives you a second chance and you really need to internalize that people have busy lives and if people don't actually use what you're building, that's fine. You can reach out to them a year from now or six months from now or two weeks from now and they probably will if you make some improvements. (00:30:37): I think people just have this fear that, "If I get a lot of rejection, that means everything is bad." But the rejection should be put in context to the early adopter idea and that most people who don't care are not early adopters, who don't want to dig into new things. And that the more narrow of a solution you have to a specific problem, the fewer people actually want to dig in. But that's where you have to start because you cannot build the whole thing right up front and make everybody loves you. That doesn't really work that way. (00:31:07): Even Airbnb was like air mattresses or staying in someone's homes when they're home. That was not the complete solution of Airbnb. But there were early adopters who dug in and be like, "Yep, I like that. I like those two things. I want to have people stay in my living room in my mattress." But that's not what Airbnb is about today, and a lot of those things were unknown at the time. But I think people are just afraid of rejection and you just need to overcome that fear and just learn that there's nothing that's really that bad that can happen when people don't use the service or sign up and don't care. It's not really that bad.
turns.zh: 是啊，我讲过这个故事，昨天刚讲过一次。还记得你第一次注册某项服务时，那是个很酷的服务，你在TechCrunch之类的平台上听说过它，然后才意识到自己一年前就注册过，对吧？而从创始人的角度看，他们会想：“大家都讨厌我，因为他们注册了却从不使用。”但用户根本没用过这项服务。这种恐惧实质上是害怕被拒绝。若你推出产品，大多数人不会用，还会跟朋友抱怨产品有多烂，劝他们别注册。但事实上，人们注册后往往会说：“哦，我很忙，有别的事要做。”他们根本不记得，也不在乎。（00:29:43）所以当你注册一年前用过的服务时，要提醒自己这是常见的用户体验——人们注册了太多东西，甚至都不记得。用户不会产生“我讨厌这个东西”的反应，而是会说：“我对这个无感，甚至懒得完成注册流程或尝试使用。”这才是人们需要记住的——初创公司最怕的不是用户讨厌你的产品，而是他们对产品无动于衷。这不是最糟糕的情况，但最常见的情况是人们就是无动于衷。但这不会给你第二次机会。比如说，用户总会给你机会改进，但你必须深刻认识到人们生活忙碌，若他们不使用你的产品，那也没关系。你可以在一年后、六个月后、两周后再联系他们，只要你有所改进，他们很可能就会回心转意。（00:30:37）我觉得人们总是害怕：“如果遭遇大量拒绝，就意味着产品很糟糕。” 但这种拒绝需要放在早期采用者的背景下看待。大多数不感兴趣的人都不是早期采用者，他们不愿深入探索新事物。解决特定问题的方案越窄，愿意深入探索的人就越少。但这正是你必须从起点开始的地方，因为你不可能一开始就做好一切，让所有人都喜欢你。这根本行不通。（00:31:07）就连Airbnb最初也只是提供充气床垫或入住他人住宅的服务。这并非Airbnb的完整解决方案。但当时有早期采用者深入研究，说：“是的，我喜欢这两个功能。我想让别人住在我的客厅，用我的床垫。” 但这不是Airbnb现在的主营业务了，当时很多功能都还不为人知。但我觉得人们就是害怕被拒绝，你只需要克服这种恐惧，明白当用户不使用你的服务或不注册、不在乎时，其实也没什么大不了的。这真的没那么糟糕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of a quote that I always love for Mark Andreessen, that everyone's time is already allocated. They don't have space for your product right now. They already have plans for their day.
turns.zh: 这让我想起马克·安德森的一句话：“每个人的时间都是有限的。他们现在没有空间给你的产品。他们已经安排好了一天的行程。”

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it takes a lot to convince someone to pay attention to anything. I guess that just comes back to why it's so important that your product is solving a real pain and not just a nice little toy that is better than what's out there, but not so much better that you're like, "I need this right now." So maybe just along those lines, do you have any thoughts on just the importance of that pain and just how critical that is?
turns.zh: 让别人关注任何事物都需要花费很大力气。我想这正说明了为什么你的产品必须要解决一个真实的痛点，而不仅仅是一个比现有产品更好的小玩意儿。但即便如此，也不至于让人感叹“我现在就需要这个”。所以，基于这个思路，你对痛点的重要性以及其关键性有什么见解吗？

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: I actually recorded... I'm happy of these videos, but I've recorded two videos on YouTube as part of YC Startup School last fall. You can go watch them on YouTube right now. One of them is how to talk to users and the other one is how you sell or how you use sales. The one about talking to users, I think there's a difference in asking someone, "Do you have a problem with X, Y, Z? Is this podcasting setup working for you?" And people say, "Yeah, it's kind of working." But if you are a podcasting setup experts and you watch people use some other thing that's really shitty, they might also think that it's pretty good. But you have to watch them do it. And the best way for you to figure out what is the intensity of the problem is not to ask them but to watch them or to watch them solve the thing that they do. (00:33:06): You know how a lot of non-technical people don't know how to automate things? So they will do the same thing in Excel like a million times by just tapping because that's the only thing that they know and they're not technical enough to write some kind of script to do it, and you just have to watch those people to just feel the pain. You can't actually ask them how difficult is it to do X, y, z because they won't even know that it's that difficult to them. So the best thing I've learned about how to discover the pain is to watch people, have them screen share, have them walk you through their daily workflow about the area where you're doing some discovery. That is the best thing. (00:33:43): I'll give you another example. So there's a bunch of waste companies that are doing EV charging for electric cars and they're like, "What are the problems in EV charging?" And I was like, "Just rent an EV and go and charge at all the non Tesla chargers and see what they say, see what you experience." And the truth is that it's just like garbage. A lot of EV charting systems are just so shitty and the apps are terrible. You just have to just use them yourself to know how bad it is.
turns.zh: 实际上我录制了……我对这些视频很满意，但去年秋天在YC创业学校上，我在YouTube上录制了两个视频。你们现在可以在YouTube上观看。其中一个是如何与用户沟通，另一个是如何销售或利用销售技巧。关于与用户沟通的那个视频，我认为问用户“你在X、Y、Z方面有问题吗？这个播客设置对你有用吗？”和让他们说“嗯，还算能用”是有区别的。但如果你是一个播客设置方面的专家，看到别人使用一些非常糟糕的设备时，他们可能也会觉得还不错。但你必须亲眼看着他们操作。要想了解问题的严重程度，问他们是没用的，最好是观察他们操作，或者观察他们解决问题时的表现。（00:33:06）：你知道很多非技术人员不知道如何自动化操作吗？所以他们会在Excel里重复做无数次同样的操作，只是因为这是他们唯一会的，又没有技术能力写脚本去实现自动化。你必须亲眼看着他们操作，才能感受到他们的痛苦。你没法问他们做X、Y、Z有多难，因为他们甚至意识不到这对他们来说有多难。所以发现痛点的最好方法就是观察人们，邀请他们进行屏幕共享，让他们演示你在做探索的领域的日常工作流程。这才是最有效的方法。（00:33:43）：我再举个例子。有很多废物管理公司在做电动汽车充电业务，他们会问：“电动汽车充电存在哪些问题？”我就会说：“去租一辆电动车，在所有非特斯拉充电桩上充电，看看他们怎么说，看看你的实际体验。” 说实话，那些充电系统简直一团糟，很多充电应用也糟糕透顶。你必须亲自使用才能知道有多糟糕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's cool how often it just comes back to, "Just go do the thing. Do things that don't scale." Classic YC advice. I want to come back to something you mentioned that I want to pull a thread on as the technical co-founder, being technical early on, just to cover that. So I know YC looks to... Having a technical founder is an important variable in you're deciding to accept a company. Say someone doesn't have a technical co-founder, do you have any advice for what they could do, like what often can work?
turns.zh: 很棒的是，很多时候答案都是“去做就行了。做那些不可扩展的事情。” 这就是YC的经典建议。我想再回到你提到的另一个点——作为技术合伙人，早期专注技术的重要性，这里就点到为止。所以我知道YC在筛选公司时，技术创始人是一个重要的考量因素。如果有人没有技术合伙人，你有什么建议他们可以怎么做，比如哪些方法通常有效？

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Yeah, I think the first thing is to understand the value of technical co-founder. So some people who are in this situation where they have an idea of something they want to build and they don't have anyone to help build them in building it, I had a friend Paul who gave this incredible quote, he said, "I have an idea for a song, I just need a musician to help me make it," right? That's kind of similar to how it is with engineering. If you view output of engineering as like, "I just have an idea for a song, I just need someone to actually make it for me" and then you're not valuing software engineering or mechanical engineering or any engineering skill set deep enough, right? (00:35:17): The truth is that the engineering part is the really hard part. The first thing I would say is you need to learn how to value the engineering piece. Let me give you an example of how you don't do that. You applied to YC and you have 90% for yourself and 10% for the engineer. You're basically saying that like, "Oh, the engineering part of this company is only worth 1/10th of me. I'm the non-technical person." So that to me is a signal that you're not really valuing engineering. (00:35:44): Okay, so how do you go out about and find someone? Well, the truth is that there are a lot of technical co-founders. The technical people, they also want to find business co-founders. They don't want to do other part. They don't want to do sales and they actually don't really care that much about fundraising. They just want to solve the problem. And that's fine. We built something called co-founder matching where those funders can meet, but if you don't participate in that, you can just start by asking the best technical people that you know. "Are you interested in starting a company with me?" Same thing with rejection. Many of them will just say, "No, I have a great job, I'm really happy." But some of them will have thought about starting a company for a while and was hoping that someone would come and ask them to do that. So you have to remove your fears and go and ask the best people. (00:36:29): The reason you want to have a technical co-founder and not a hired engineer or not a hired contracting team is because so many of the decisions you're going to make are technical and so many of the iterations you're going to make relies on engineering. And if you don't understand that, you won't actually make the right decisions anyway. It's not like service. You have an idea for a product, you build a product and you're done. There's infinite number of iterations in that process. (00:36:54): And then finally, I would say a lot of people learn how to code themselves, right? So there are a lot of places online that you can learn the skillset that takes to build a prototype. You might not be the best engineers. So there are many successful startup founders who are not the best engineers because they stop coding when they hire three or four engineers, that's fine. But you need to be sufficiently good that you understand the value of engineering and that you understand that the best way to solve most of the problem is with software. There are a lot of founders who just, for whatever reason, study something else that doesn't have to be a conscious or very precise reason that you had when you were 18 or 19 and then you're 25, you're like, "Oh, I wish I know how to code" and then just learn to code and they learn how to code. It's not that more difficult than that.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为首先要理解技术联合创始人的价值。所以有些人处于这样的境地——他们有想开发的产品，但找不到人来帮忙实现。我的朋友保罗曾说过一句很棒的话：“我有个歌曲创意，只是需要一位音乐人帮我把它做出来。”这和工程领域的情况很相似。如果你把工程成果视为“我有个歌曲创意，只是需要别人帮我实现”，那你就低估了软件工程、机械工程或任何工程技能的价值，对吧？（00:35:17）：事实上，工程部分才是真正难的部分。我首先要说的是，你需要学会如何重视工程部分。让我举个反面例子：你向YC申请融资，90%归你自己，10%归工程师。这等于在说：“这家公司的工程部分只值我自己的十分之一。我是非技术人员。”在我看来，这就是不重视工程的表现。（00:35:44）：好的，那怎么才能找到合适的人呢？事实上，技术联合创始人很多。他们也想找到商业联合创始人。他们不想负责销售和融资，只想解决问题。这没关系。我们开发了一个叫“联合创始人匹配”的平台，让双方能对接，但如果你不参与这个平台，你可以先问问你认识的最优秀的技术人员：“你有兴趣和我一起创业吗？”面对拒绝也要坦然。很多人会说：“不了，我现在工作很好，很开心。”但有些人可能已经考虑创业很久，期待有人来邀请他们。所以你要克服恐惧，主动去问最优秀的人。（00:36:29）：为什么要找技术联合创始人，而不是雇佣工程师或承包团队？因为很多决策和迭代都需要技术支持。如果你不理解这一点，就无法做出正确决策。这和服务行业不同。服务行业是有了产品概念就能直接做，但创业过程中迭代无数次。（00:36:54）：最后，很多人自学编程，对吧？网上有很多资源能教你开发原型所需的技能。你不一定是顶尖工程师。很多成功的创业者并非最优秀的工程师，因为他们雇佣三四名工程师后就不再编程了。这没关系，但你至少要足够优秀，理解工程的价值，明白用软件解决问题是最佳方案。很多创业者因为各种原因（不一定是18、19岁时就有的清晰规划），25岁时才想学编程然后自学成功。这比想象中容易得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you ever seen a startup work out if they had a contracting firm, like engineering firm build a product? Does that ever work or were you just like, "No, do not ever do this"?
turns.zh: 你们有没有见过创业公司让外包公司，比如工程公司来开发产品？这种方式可行吗？还是说你们当时会直接说“不行，还是别这么做”？

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Basically, I can't recall any specific ones where people have a contracting firm but I've recalled founders where let's say you had two non-technical founders, but they valued engineering and they had an ability to build a team of great people that were not co-founders and they gave them equity and they become successful. There are many examples of that I would say, but I don't remember any specific examples where you had a contracting team building the whole thing. I think the reason for that is it takes more than just sort of riding a spec to build a product. You can't actually spec yourself to a great product. You have to just be part of the iterations yourself. That's why I think someone being the engineer, having the idea of what iteration looks like and just doing it is how you do things. (00:38:38): I think that the cases where I've seen non-technical founders make this work is that they have really good engineering teams who feel like they're founding team. It might not be co-founders per YC-7 definition of having 10%, but they feel like they're the bonding team.
turns.zh: 基本上，我记不起来有哪家公司让外包公司开发产品，但我倒是记得有些创业者——比如说有两个非技术型创始人，但他们重视工程技术，并且有能力组建一支非联合创始人的优秀团队，给他们股份，最终取得了成功。这样的例子有很多，但我不记得有哪家公司完全让外包团队来开发整个产品。我认为原因在于，打造一款产品需要的远不止是纸上谈兵。你不可能仅凭想象就打造出一款出色的产品，必须亲身参与产品的迭代过程。这就是为什么我认为，由工程师主导产品开发、亲自把控迭代流程才是正确的做法。（00:38:38）：我见过非技术型创始人成功案例的，他们拥有非常优秀的工程团队，这些团队感觉自己就是创始团队。虽然按照YC7 10%股权的定义，他们不算联合创始人，但他们确实把自己视为团队的核心成员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of a story of just the recent podcast interview I did with the CPO of Calendly. She talked about how when Calendly started, they actually had a Ukrainian dev team built the first product. Not only did they help them build the first product, they actually ended up driving all the growth initially because they saw Calendly and started using it within their firm.
turns.zh: 这让我想起最近我采访Calendly首席产品官的播客内容。她提到Calendly刚成立时，实际上是由一支乌克兰开发团队开发的首款产品。这支团队不仅帮助他们完成了首款产品的开发，还在初期推动了产品的增长，因为他们在自己的公司内部率先使用了Calendly。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then everyone that they knew started using it and spread within Ukraine and they actually continue to work with that firm. They're still the [inaudible 00:39:20] team for Calendly or some part of it.
turns.zh: 然后他们认识的每个人都开始使用它，在乌克兰范围内传播开来，至今仍在与这家公司合作。他们仍然是Calendly的[听不清00:39:20]团队或其中的某个部分。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah
turns.zh: 是啊

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: Wow, that's cool.
turns.zh: 哇，真酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a success story.
turns.zh: 这确实是个成功案例。

turns.speaker: Gustaf Alströmer
turns.en: I mean, I would say it's certainly the case that in some countries people have other jobs while they start the startups, so like the engineers. In Ukraine for example or in Eastern Europe, it's very common that if they start their own startup, they actually have a full-time job as a contractor while they're starting the startup because that's how you pay the bill because often you can't raise money. And that's fine too.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我认为在某些国家，比如乌克兰或东欧，人们在创业初期确实会兼职做其他工作来维持生计。比如工程师们在那里很常见，如果他们创办自己的初创公司，通常会一边找全职工作做外包，一边创业，因为这样才能维持生计，毕竟很多时候初创公司很难融资。这种模式也无可厚非。
